paragraphs: §1 — The prooftexts of those who deny the resurrection, and their construal of the resurrection-verses as figurative

A group of those who profess Judaism (man yantaḥil al-yahūdiyya) invalidate the resurrection of the dead (iḥyāʾ al-amwāt), and they ground what they claim of that upon passages of Scripture. That is, for instance, the saying of דוד (peace be upon him) [Ps 103:16] כי רוח עברה בו ואיננו ולא יכירנו עוד מקומו ("for a wind passes over it and it is gone, and its place knows it no more"), and the saying of Asaph [Ps 78:39] ויזכר כי בשר המה רוח הולך ולא ישוב ("and He remembered that they were flesh, a breath that goes and does not return"). They said: so by this saying He stated explicitly that, when the spirits of human beings depart, there is no return for them. And likewise the saying of Job [Job 14:14] אם ימות גבר היחיה ("if a man dies, shall he live?"), and his saying [Job 14:12] ואיש שכב ולא יקום ("and a man lies down and does not rise"), and his saying also [Job 7:9-10] לא ישוב עוד לביתו ולא יכירנו עוד מקומו ("he shall not return again to his house, and his place shall know him no more"), and his saying [Job 10:21] בטרם אלך ולא אשוב ("before I go, never to return"). They said: since the texts have spoken thus and have reported that whoever dies does not live [again], the statement of whoever claims that the dead live [again] is a false statement. And they claimed, concerning what we have already mentioned [the deniers say] of His saying [Dan 12:2] ורבים מישני אדמת עפר יקיצו ("and many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake"), and His saying [Isa 26:19] יחיו מתיך נבלתי יקומון ("your dead shall live, my corpses shall rise"), and His saying [Ps 104:30] תשלח רוחך יבראון ("You send forth Your spirit, they are created"), and His saying [Ezek 37:12] פתח את קברותיכם ("[I will] open your graves") — that all of that is not according to its literal sense, but rather the purport of it is the return of the exile (al-jāliya) and the reviving of the nation from the abasement and contempt it is in; for Scripture admits of no contradiction (al-tanāquḍ), and since it has stated in more than one place that whoever dies does not return, it is established that its reporting in another place that the dead live [again] is not according to its literal sense, but rather its meaning is what we have said.

: The preamble lays out the deniers' case in the catalogue-then-refute manner Q used in Babs 5–6. The deniers' opponents (the resurrection-affirmers) are Q's own party; the deniers reverse the figurative/literal assignment, reading the "no-return" verses (Pss 103:16, 78:39; Job 14:14, 14:12, 7:9-10, 10:21) as literal and the resurrection verses (Dan 12:2; Isa 26:19; Ps 104:30; Ezek 37:12) as figurative — figures for the national revival, the return of al-jāliya (the exilic community) from dhull (abasement). The governing premise is the same anti-contradiction axiom Q himself uses throughout the Maqala (al-kitāb lā yajūz ʿalayhi al-tanāquḍ) — which is precisely why Q will turn it back on them in §2.
§2 — Turning the anti-contradiction principle against the deniers; the decisive cases of Elisha and Daniel

So it is to be said to them: if the resurrection of the dead is invalidated in your view — despite what the texts have reported of it — only because the text, in your view, has reported the contrary of that in another place, since contradiction is not admissible of Scripture, then why have you made it obligatory that His withholding of life from the dead be according to its literal sense, while you have carried His granting of that onto interpretation (al-taʾwīl)? And why have you not set the affirmation according to its literal sense, and carried the withholding onto interpretation — since reason does not preclude that [resurrection], together with the agreement of the whole nation upon it, none having dissented in it save one who has waxed insolent and feigned ignorance?

And if some fancier should fancy that this our statement entails the equivalence of the two sayings and their being on a par (takāfuʾ al-qawlayn wa-tawāzīhimā) — then that which corroborates our statement and invalidates the statement of our opponents is what אֱלִישָׁע did in reviving the son of הַשּׁוּנַמִּית (the Shunammite), and likewise the revival of the man who was cast into the grave of אֱלִשָׁע, of whom it says [2 Kgs 13:21] בנגע ויחי ויקם על רגליו ("at the touch he revived and stood up on his feet"). These two reports admit of no interpretation [otherwise]; rather they are according to their literal sense beyond doubt. And what also corroborates that and verifies it — that the saying of God (exalted be He) in the Prophets [Dan 12:2] דניאל מישני אדמת עפר יקיצו is according to its literal sense, namely that the dead live [again] — is His saying to him [Daniel] after that [Dan 12:13] ואתה לך לקץ ותנוח ותעמד לגורלך לקץ הימין ("but you, go your way to the end; you shall rest and shall stand up for your lot at the end of days"). For He informed him that he too is among those who live [again] at that time; and He did not intend by that that He delivers him from the exile (al-jalāʾ) nor from the abasement, since he was not present at that time. Moreover, some of the indications by which He indicated the resurrection of the dead admit of no interpretation [otherwise], namely His saying [Ps 104:30] תשלח רוחך יבראון — and that is according to what we expounded in the bab before this one.

: The hinge of the bab: the deniers cannot non-arbitrarily privilege the "no-return" verses as literal and demote the resurrection verses to figure. The anti-contradiction principle cuts both ways; absent a reason to prefer one assignment, the literal/figurative distribution is underdetermined. Q presses two further considerations: reason does not bar bodily resurrection (so the rational presumption favoring non-literal readings of the impossible does not apply), and the consensus (ijmāʿ) of "the whole nation" affirms it — Q's tighaṭrasa wa-tajāhala ("waxed insolent and feigned ignorance") is his standing polemical register for the lone dissenter (cf. al-ḥayārā in the glossary §VIII–IX).

: Q forestalls the objection that his §2 argument merely shows takāfuʾ (equipollence) of the two readings — a stalemate. He breaks the tie with cases that cannot be figurative: the two Elisha resurrections (2 Kgs 4, the Shunammite's son; 2 Kgs 13:21, the corpse revived in Elisha's tomb), which are narrative report, not prophecy admitting taʾwīl. The address to Daniel (Dan 12:13) is decisive because Daniel, long dead by the end of days, can only "stand up for his lot" by literal resurrection — the national-revival reading is excluded since Daniel "was not present at that time." The back-reference is to Bab 7's treatment of Ps 104:30 (teshallaḥ ruḥaka yibbareʾun).
§3 — The positive interpretation of the deniers' prooftexts

As for the interpretation of what they themselves adduced as a ground, of that which gives the impression that the dead do not return: the meaning of His saying [Ps 103:16] ולא יכיר עוד מקומו ("[a man] goes, and his place knows him no more") — He intended by it that the human being, when he dies, does not return to the world in the state he was in before he died: his being in his dwelling in the manner he was in at first, in the cultivation of the world and the conduct of affairs in it. Rather he lives [again] only in order to attain reward or punishment (al-thawāb aw al-ʿiqāb); and that is evident from the saying itself. The like of that is his saying [Job 7:10] לא ישוב עוד לביתו ולא יכירנו עוד מקומו ("he shall not return again to his house, and his place shall not know him again"). The like of that, it is admissible to say, [applies] in his saying [Job 14:14] כמו שנאמר ואם ימות גבר היחיה ("as it is said, 'and if a man dies, shall he live?'") — though it has also been said concerning that that its meaning is that the human being, when he dies, is not able to revive himself or to live until the Maker (mighty and exalted) revives him. The like of that is [Job 7:9] כלה ענן וילך כן יורד שאול לא יעלה ("as a cloud is consumed and goes away, so he who goes down to Sheol shall not come up"). As for his saying [Job 14:12] ואיש שכב ולא יקום ("and a man lies down and does not rise") — the meaning in it has been expounded at its end by his saying [Job 14:12] עד בלתי שמים לא יקיצו ולא יעורו משנתם ("until the heavens are no more they shall not awake nor be roused from their sleep"). So he reported that the dead do not live [again] so long as the heaven endures; but when God (mighty and exalted) renews the world (jaddada al-ʿālam), then they live [again]. And that is the meaning of the saying of דוד [Ps 104:30] תשלח רוחך יבראון ותחדש פני אדמה ("You send forth Your spirit, they are created, and You renew the face of the ground") — except that, had it been said concerning this what was said concerning that which preceded, it would [also] be admissible.

: Q's exegetical core: the "no-return" verses do not deny resurrection but deny return to the present mundane life — the deceased does not resume "the cultivation of the world (ʿimārat al-ʿālam) and the conduct of affairs," because resurrection is for eschatological reward and punishment (al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb, the Maqala III–VI eschatology — see glossary §VI), not for a second worldly career. The Job 14:12 prooftext is turned against the deniers: its own continuation ("until the heavens are no more") makes the no-rising temporary, conditioned on the un-renewed cosmos; once God "renews the world" (read into Ps 104:30's u-teḥaddesh penei adamah), resurrection follows. Q offers an alternative gloss on Job 14:14 (man cannot self-revive; only the Creator revives him) and notes the two readings are interchangeable.
§4 — The denial-from-the-four-elements, and the carpenter-and-the-bed reply

And some of them have denied that [resurrection] from the standpoint of reason and sense-perception (al-ʿaql wa-l-ḥiss); that is, [one of them] alleged that the return of bodies is impossible, since they are compounded of the four elements (al-ʿanāṣir al-arbaʿa) — namely fire, water, earth, and air. He said: so when the human being dies and his body comes to decay and dust, each one of the [elements] that was in it returns to its origin, and its return [to compounded form] has [thereby] become impossible. But the one who says this has touched upon something of unbelief (al-ilḥād); for the One who compounded these [bodies] out of those elements only took portions of them and compounded [the body] out of them — so when it decays and each one of them returns to its origin, it is not [too] hard for the Creator (mighty be His mention), and He is not incapable, to take those very portions and restore them to the like of what they were in of the first compounding. Then that second body is the very first body itself, even though the first compounding has passed away from it and a second compounding has come to be in it. That is like a carpenter who set about a door or a bed, took it apart from its compounded state, and separated its portions, then compounded it a second compounding and restored it to what it was at first: it is not said that this bed is other than that first bed — rather it is the very same, [now] compounded [anew].

: The philosophical denial (resurrection is impossible because the body's four elements disperse to their natural places and cannot recombine) is met with the standard kalām reply, identical in structure to the Bahshamī iʿāda (re-creation) argument: the Creator who first assembled the body from those elemental portions can reassemble those same portions (bi-aʿyānihā), and numerical identity is preserved across decomposition and recomposition — the reassembled body is the original. Q's carpenter-and-bed analogy (the dismantled-then-reassembled bed remains the same bed) is the homely illustration of identity-through-recomposition. The charge that the elemental denier "has touched upon ilḥād" (unbelief/heresy) marks the position as not merely mistaken but impious, since it impugns divine omnipotence. al-iʿāda is among the eschatology anchor-terms staged in glossary §VI.
§5 — The objection from bodily flux (nutrition), and the gold-and-mercury reply

And likewise they also ask, saying: it is the way of the body that there forever dissolve from it portions which nourishment (al-ghidhāʾ) replaces and restores; so what is the account of those portions that have dissolved away, and how is it admissible that they return to the body? The answer to that is like the answer regarding what was mentioned before concerning the elements — namely that the Maker (mighty and exalted) gathers those portions by His power and conjoins them with the body. And this, even had there been no semblance of it in the visible world (al-shāhid), would not be denied of the power of God — how much the more when a parallel for it is indeed found in the visible world: for were a mithqāl of gold filed down and dissolved and mixed into much dust, the extraction of that gold from that dust by mercury (al-ziʾbaq) would be feasible; and since God (blessed and exalted) created mercury by His power and placed in it a power for discerning that [gold] and extracting it, it is not denied that He is able to discern those portions mingled with the dust and to join them to the prepared body. And were a dirham's weight of saffron cast into much water, it would be submerged until nothing of it appeared — yet we know that it is present in it beyond doubt, even though it does not appear.

: §5 completes on Nemoy p253 (the top of the Bab 9 file, before the al-bāb al-tāsiʿ heading) — there is no lacuna; the bab's tail simply spilled past the Bab 8 page-range into the Bab 9 file. The objection is the standard al-takāthuf wa-l-taḥallul (accretion-and-dissolution) puzzle: bodily matter is in constant flux through metabolism, so which matter is resurrected? Q answers with the omnipotence-plus-visible-parallel structure of kalām iʿāda: God reassembles the very dispersed portions, and the claim is made plausible by two shāhid (this-worldly) analogies — the recovery of dissolved gold from dust by mercury (an alchemical commonplace, gold-mercury amalgamation), and saffron dissolved invisibly but really in water. The point of both is that imperceptible dispersal is not annihilation: the parts persist and can be regathered.
§6 — Numerical identity is preserved through dissolution and recomposition

And if a claimant claims that, when the body dissolves and decays, and then God restores those portions that had [meanwhile] rejoined their elements, it is not that first body — so that this rewarded-and-punished body would have to be other than that body which earned [its desert] — he is [thereby] obliged [to grant] that the body which exists today is not the one that existed yesterday, since from yesterday to today portions have dissolved from it and portions other than those have come to be in it. So if it is the very same [body] despite the passing-away of portions and the coming-to-be of others — since the corporeality (al-jismiyya) and the substantiality (al-jawhariyya) remain — then likewise it is the very same even when its portions have been separated and then restored, since the corporeality and the substance remain identically [intact]. So let us [now] follow this up with the discourse on the eternalization of reward and punishment (taʾbīd al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb).

: Q's decisive identity argument and the bridge to Bab 9. The objector who denies that the reassembled body is the same body (and so denies that the resurrected body can justly bear the reward/punishment earned by the living body) is impaled on an everyday fact: the living body already undergoes continuous turnover of matter, yet is uncontroversially the same body day to day. If diachronic identity survives ordinary metabolic flux — because jismiyya (corporeality) and jawhar (substance) persist — then it survives death-and-resurrection equally, for the same reason. This is the Bahshamī criterion of personal identity (continuity of the underlying jawhar, not of token particles), and it secures the justice of bodily reward and punishment. The closing sentence (fa-li-nattabiʿ … bi-l-qawl fī taʾbīd al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb) is the explicit transition to Bab 9, "On the eternalization of reward and punishment."

- The bab's subject and adversary. The heading is unambiguous: fī al-radd ʿalā man abṭala iḥyāʾ al-amwāt — "on refuting whoever invalidated the resurrection of the dead." The adversaries are identified only as "a group of those who profess Judaism" (qawm mimman yantaḥil al-yahūdiyya) — Q's careful distancing phrase (they profess Judaism, i.e., are nominally Jews but heterodox on this point). This matches the resurrection-denying current Q associates elsewhere with Sadducee-descended sectarians; the position is intra-Jewish, not the Christian adversary of Babs 1–7. Note the structural pivot from the anti-Christian polemic of Babs 1–7 to intra-Jewish eschatological controversy in Bab 8 — fitting the eschatology block (thawāb / ʿiqāb) the glossary stages for §VI (M3 B7–12).

- The anti-contradiction principle, turned. The deniers' argument and Q's reply share a single premise — al-kitāb lā yajūz ʿalayhi al-tanāquḍ ("Scripture admits no contradiction"). The deniers use it to demote the resurrection verses to figure; Q uses it to show their literal/figurative assignment is arbitrary (§2), and breaks the resulting takāfuʾ (equipollence) with non-prophetic, hence non-figurable, narrative cases (the two Elisha resurrections) and the personally-addressed Daniel 12:13. This is exactly the taʾwīl-as-farʿ-of-aṣl hermeneutic of Bab 6 §1, here applied to an intra-Jewish dispute.

- The "renewal of the world" eschatology. Q's controlling exegetical move (§3) is that the "no-return" verses deny resumption of mundane life, not resurrection: the dead return not to ʿimārat al-ʿālam but for al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb. He times resurrection to the cosmic renewal (read out of Job 14:12's "until the heavens are no more" + Ps 104:30's "You renew the face of the ground"). This sets up the reward/punishment eschatology of the following babs.

- The iʿāda argument (§§4–6). The four-elements denial and the recomposition reply are textbook kalām iʿāda (bodily re-creation): the carpenter/bed analogy (§4), the bodily-flux objection answered by the gold-from-dust-by-mercury and the dissolved-saffron analogies (§5), and the criterion of identity-through-recomposition (§6) — numerically the same body persists so long as jismiyya and jawhar persist, exactly as the living body persists through ordinary metabolic turnover. This is the Bahshamī position; the analogies are Q's own concretizations. Worth noting that Q frames the elemental denial as bordering on ilḥād — an unusually sharp charge, reserved for a position that limits divine power. §6's closing sentence is the explicit bridge to Bab 9 (taʾbīd al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb).

- For the kalām iʿāda (bodily resurrection / re-creation) doctrine and the four-elements objection: ʿAbd al-Jabbār, al-Mughnī vol. on al-Maʿād (and Sharḥ al-Uṣūl al-Khamsa on al-iʿāda); the Bahshamī argument that God reassembles the very same dispersed parts is the direct parallel to Q here. See glossary §VI anchor terms (iʿāda, thawāb, ʿiqāb). - For the Jewish resurrection-denial current Q targets: Q's own Anwar Maqala I treatment of the sects (the Sadducees / al-Ṣadūqiyya and their denial of resurrection); Leon Nemoy, "Al-Qirqisānī's Account of the Jewish Sects," HUCA 7 (1930). For the broader medieval Jewish resurrection debate, Saadia, Kitāb al-Amānāt wa-l-Iʿtiqādāt, treatise VII (On the Revival of the Dead), which argues the literal-resurrection case on closely comparable scriptural and rational grounds. - For the Karaite eschatological tradition: Daniel Frank, Search Scripture Well (2004) on Yefet ben ʿEli's treatment of the resurrection verses (Dan 12:2; Isa 26:19; Ezek 37); Haggai Ben-Shammai on Qirqisānī's and Yefet's Muʿtazilī eschatology. - For the back-reference to Ps 104:30: Bab 7 of this Maqala (the bab "before this one"), where teshallaḥ ruḥaka yibbareʾun is expounded as a non-figurable resurrection indicator.
